paras: The threatened lynching of Paul Bates took place in Screven County, Georgia, where Bates, a Black tenant charged with killing Grady Oliver, nearly was lynched in jail before troops were called out against a mob. Bates was then tried under military guard and hanged in May 1919; the Savannah Tribune argued that no fair trial was possible under a mob's threat.

The Savannah Tribune described the case as typical of the clashes between "the white landlord and his Negro tenant" in rural Georgia. Bates testified that the dead man and his brother had abused and threatened him in a wagon the day before the homicide.

While Bates was held in the jail at "Syllanja," a mob came close to lynching him, and the military was called out to prevent it. He was kept in Savannah for safekeeping before and after his trial, held at an extra session of court under guard of Augusta and Newington troops. No witnesses testified for him; the Tribune said anyone with favorable testimony would have risked being lynched.
He was sentenced to death, and his appointed counsel filed no motion for a new trial, saying Bates would have been lynched on the spot otherwise.

Lawyers who took up the case afterward obtained three respites from the governor, moving the execution date from February to May 23. Their extraordinary motion for a new trial was before the Screven court on May 19, but the judge fell ill and the court adjourned until June without hearing it. Despite statements from prominent Screven County men, the governor refused to commute the sentence or grant a stay, and Bates was hanged, "protesting, that he acted in self-defence."

The only coverage found is an editorial in the Savannah Tribune of May 31, 1919, headed "The Truth About Paul Bates." The paper called Bates "the hapless victim of fate and circumstances" and wrote that in such cases the law was "helpless before race hate." It argued that the troops and "the threatening mob which it is brought out to restrain" made a fair trial impossible, and that the governor should have intervened.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Paul Bates
bases: The Savannah Tribune reports that Bates came near to being lynched in jail and that troops were called out to restrain a threatening mob, a threatened lynching followed by a legal execution (A4, A5).

Bates was not killed by the mob; the Tribune says he was hanged under a court's death sentence after troops prevented a lynching, so the killing had lawful authority, though the mob threatened him over the homicide charge (A4, A5).
The only report found is one two-part Savannah Tribune editorial (A4, A5).

accounts.label: Savannah Tribune editorial
accounts.gist: Bates nearly was lynched, was tried under troops amid mob threats without defense witnesses, and was hanged after legal technicalities and the governor's refusal closed his last chances; he said he killed in self-defense.

framing.detail: Headlined 'The Truth About Paul Bates', the editorial says the law is 'helpless before race hate' and that a trial under military guard and a threatening mob cannot be fair.

record_check.dossier: Near-lynching undated; execution set for May 23, 1919, and reported as 'last week' on May 31.
Black: the editorial treats the case as a clash between 'the white landlord and his Negro tenant'.

record_check.record: accused of killing Grady Oliver, his white landlord
record_check.dossier: Charged with and convicted of killing 'Grady Ou- ver'; the paper implies but does not say outright that the dead man was his landlord.

record_check.record: convicted and sentenced to death; military called out
record_check.dossier: Add that Bates was legally hanged the week before May 31, 1919, after three respites and the governor's refusal of clemency.
'Syllanja' as printed in the OCR text; the only place named for the jail.

info: Date of the near-lynching not given; Bates was sentenced before February 1919 and, after three respites, set to hang May 23, 1919; the Tribune of May 31 says he was hanged 'last week'.
The jail at 'Syllanja' (as printed), Screven County; Bates was held in Savannah for safekeeping before and after the trial.
Paul Bates, described as a Negro tenant in a landlord-tenant clash.
Charged with the murder of 'Grady Ou- ver' (OCR; Oliver); Bates said he acted in self-defense after the dead man and his brother abused and threatened him in a wagon the day before.
An unnamed 'threatening mob'; no names or numbers given.
Governor granted three respites; extraordinary motion for a new trial not heard after judge fell ill May 19; governor refused commutation and a stay; Bates hanged the week before May 31, 1919.

sources.note: Editorial 'The Truth About Paul Bates': near-lynching in Syllanja jail, military called out, trial under troops, death sentence, no new-trial motion for fear of lynching, three respites.
quotes: He came near to being lynched while incarcerated in the Syllanja jail, the military being called out to prevent this.
Paul Bates was tried for murder in an atmosphere of mob violence and lynching.
Bates would have been lynched that day on the spot if such motion had been made or if the verdict had been other than death.

sources.note: Continuation of the editorial: motion stalled when judge fell ill May 19, governor refused commutation or stay, Bates died protesting self-defense.
quotes: Paul Bates died, protesting, that he acted in self-defence and there are many who will always share that view.
The Governor refused to commute the sentence to life imprisonment, and refused to grant a stay of execution
